items.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, September 23, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Miles Davis is mentioned by the interviewer as a respondent to Walter Cronkite, and later by the interviewee as an example of a musician whose roots are often cited, but the interviewee does not describe a personal interaction or direct professional relationship with Miles Davis.

ctx.x: But you have a very distinct voice on that instrument. You’ve taken that instrument past any generic conception into this elusive category that all musicians seek called “voice.” And you have that.

Thank you. That I think is a prerequisite for anybody doing anything, is to put their “John Hancock” you know, once you’ve seen that signature it’s forever imprinted on your mind. And I think the only way you can ever establish yourself is to have something like the cookie cutter, according to that syndrome, is you must take it upon yourself to bite the bullet and say, for better or for worse, this is the way I sound. This is the sound that I make. And you must stand by it. And that’s why this, you know “you’re…

items.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Even Miles Davis’ parents, you know, didn’t condone jazz music...

ctx.x: There’s some people in jazz who teach it who feel like jazz started with John Coltrane.

Correct. Certainly. Those poor fools haven’t got a clue I’m sorry to say. I mean if you want to teach jazz you take it back to where it’s able to be taught from and when it’s the most understandable, when it was still part of the popular culture, where the kids, that was their music. They were the rebels. Their parents looked at that kind of music, oh that’s awful, dreadful, jazz music. Even Miles Davis’ parents, you know, didn’t condone jazz music because it was the devil’s music, it was this kind of music, it…
